claims.source: This nucleus is also known for participating in hippocampal theta rhythm (Pan and McNaughton, 2002; Pan and McNaughton, 1997), possibly by its direct projection to the hippocampus or by modulation of the medial septum (Borhegyi et al., 1998; Vertes and Kocsis, 1997), and regulating spike-timing between hippocampus and the cortex (Ito et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Disruption of SuM neuron activity with pharmacological methods has been reported to disrupt hippocampal memory.
claims.source: Disruption of SuM neuron activity with pharmacological methods (Aranda et al., 2008; Shahidi et al., 2004) or lesions (Aranda et al., 2006) has been reported to disrupt hippocampal memory.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Serotonin depletion of the SuM leads to deficiencies in spatial learning in the Morris water maze.
claims.source: Serotonin depletion of the SuM leads to deficiencies in spatial learning in the Morris water maze, and results in altered hippocampal theta activity (Gutiérrez-Guzmán et al., 2012; Hernández-Pérez et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Salient rewarding experiences activate the SuM, as evidenced by cFos expression in monoaminergic SuM neurons by consumption of rewarding food.
claims.source: Salient rewarding experiences also activate the SuM, as evidenced by cFos expression in monoaminergic SuM neurons by consumption of rewarding food (Plaisier et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: The rewarding aspects of social aggression involve an excitatory circuit between the hypothalamic ventral premammillary nucleus and the SuM.
claims.source: Furthermore, the rewarding aspects of social aggression have been shown to involve an excitatory circuit between the hypothalamic ventral premammillary nucleus and the SuM (Stagkourakis et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: There are two separate populations of cells in the SuM that target either CA2 or the DG.
claims.source: It has recently been shown that there are two separate populations of cells in the SuM that target either CA2 or the DG (Chen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claims.claim: In the DG, the SuM terminals release both glutamate and GABA.
claims.source: In the DG, the SuM terminals release both glutamate and GABA (Boulland et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2020; Hashimotodani et al., 2018; Pedersen et al., 2017; Soussi et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The SuM-DG projection plays a role in modulating DG activity in response to contextual novelty.
claims.source: The SuM-DG projection has been recently shown to play a role in modulating DG activity in response to contextual novelty (Chen et al., 2020) and spatial memory retrieval (Li et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to recent research.

claims.claim: Functional studies of the SuM-CA2 projection have found that this connection is entirely glutamatergic.
claims.source: In contrast, functional studies of the SuM-CA2 projection have found that this connection is entirely glutamatergic (Chen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claims.claim: The CA2-projecting SuM neurons are active during social novelty exposure.
claims.source: It was recently discovered that the CA2-projecting SuM neurons are active during social novelty exposure, and their selective stimulation prevents expression of a memory of a familiar conspecific (Chen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claims.claim: Selective stimulation of CA2-projecting SuM neurons prevents expression of a memory of a familiar conspecific.
claims.source: It was recently discovered that the CA2-projecting SuM neurons are active during social novelty exposure, and their selective stimulation prevents expression of a memory of a familiar conspecific (Chen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claims.claim: A subset of SuM neurons were active earlier than CA2 and other hippocampal cells during SWR.
claims.source: Furthermore, recent in vivo recordings from the SuM in anesthetized rats reported that a subset of SuM neurons were active earlier than CA2 and other hippocampal cells during SWR (Vicente et al., 2020), indicating a possible role for the SuM-CA2 projection in shaping area CA2 activity prior to SWR onset.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research.

claims.claim: The source of vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGluT2)-immunopositive boutons in area CA2 originate from the SuM.
claims.source: It has been shown that the source of vesicular glutamate transporter 2 (VGluT2)-immunopositive boutons in area CA2 originate from the SuM (Halasy et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: CA2-projecting cells express calretinin and are located in the medial SuM.
claims.source: Consistent with recent findings using retrograde AAV vectors (Chen et al., 2020), we observed that CA2-projecting cells express calretinin and are located in the medial SuM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by both citation to recent research and immunohistochemical data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: CA2-projecting SuM cells are located bilaterally, ventral to the fiber bundles that traverse the SuM.
claims.source: These cells were located bilaterally, ventral to the fiber bundles that traverse the SuM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: CA2-projecting SuM cells stain for VGluT2.
claims.source: Furthermore, we confirmed that these cells also stain for VGluT2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: EYFP-containing SuM axons were found throughout the granule cell layer of the DG and in area CA2.
claims.source: EYFP-containing SuM axons were found throughout the granule cell layer of the DG and in area CA2 (Figure 1B) where they clustered around the pyramidal layer (stratum pyramidale, SP).
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The SuM fiber projection area was clearly restricted to area CA2, as defined by expression of the CA2-specific markers PCP4 and RGS14.
claims.source: The SuM fiber projection area was clearly restricted to area CA2, as defined by expression of the CA2-specific markers PCP4 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) and RGS14 (Figure 1B), and did not spread to neighboring areas CA3 and CA1.
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of SuM axons elicited excitatory post-synaptic responses in 63% of PNs located in area CA2.
claims.source: We observed that photostimulation of SuM axons elicited excitatory post-synaptic responses in 63% of PNs (n = 166 of 263 cells) located in area CA2.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: The SuM-PN connectivity was not different between CA2 and CA3 PNs.
claims.source: We found that the SuM-PN connectivity was not different between CA2 and CA3 PNs (Table 2, χ² test for CA2 and CA3 PNs, p=0.572)
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: The SuM-PN connectivity was not different between deep and superficial PNs.
claims.source: We found that the SuM-PN connectivity was not different between CA2 and CA3 PNs (Table 2, χ² test for CA2 and CA3 PNs, p=0.572) or between deep and superficial PNs (Table 2, χ² test for deep and superficial PNs, p=0.946).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Light-evoked excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) and excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) recorded at −70 mV were of fairly small amplitude.
claims.source: Light-evoked excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) and excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) recorded at −70 mV were of fairly small amplitude (Figure 1C–D)
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figures.

claims.claim: The amplitude of SuM input-evoked post-synaptic responses was similar regardless of the PN type or somatic location.
claims.source: Light-evoked excitatory post-synaptic potentials (EPSPs) and excitatory post-synaptic currents (EPSCs) recorded at −70 mV were of fairly small amplitude (Figure 1C–D) that were similar regardless of the PN type or somatic location (Table 2, Mann-Whitney U test for CA2 and CA3 PNs, p=0.409; Mann-Whitney U test for deep and superficial PNs, p=0.306).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: All SuM transmission was blocked following application of the sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX).
claims.source: We are confident that this transmission is due to action potential-generated vesicle release because all transmission was blocked following application of the sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The pure glutamatergic nature of the SuM input was confirmed by the complete block of light-evoked synaptic transmission following the application of the AMPA and NMDA receptors antagonists NBQX and D-APV.
claims.source: The pure glutamatergic nature of the SuM input was confirmed by the complete block of light-evoked synaptic transmission following the application of the AMPA and NMDA receptors antagonists NBQX and D-APV (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; amplitudes were −16 ± 4.8 pA in control and −1.8 ± 0.3 pA in NBQX and D-APV, n = 6; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.03).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: SuM inputs provide long-range glutamatergic excitation to CA2 and CA3 PNs in area CA2.
claims.source: These data confirm that SuM inputs provide long-range glutamatergic excitation to CA2 and CA3 PNs in area CA2.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented.

claims.claim: Blocking inhibitory transmission with the GABAA and GABAB receptor antagonists SR95531 and CGP55845A led to a significant increase of light-evoked PSP amplitude recorded in area CA2 PNs.
claims.source: Interestingly, blocking inhibitory transmission with the GABAA and GABAB receptor antagonists SR95531 and CGP55845A led to a significant increase of light-evoked PSP amplitude recorded in area CA2 PNs (Figure 2A–C; amplitudes of the first response were 0.18 ± 0.05 mV in control and 0.24 ± 0.05 mV in SR95531 and CGP55845A, n = 14; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, p=0.004 for the first PSP, p=0.013 for the second PSP, p<0.001 for the third PSP).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: SuM-driven excitation is negatively controlled by feedforward inhibition.
claims.source: Thus, this result demonstrates a negative control of SuM-driven excitation by feedforward inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing increased PSP amplitude when inhibition is blocked.

claims.claim: SuM input stimulation paired with SR input had a net depolarizing effect when CA2 PNs were kept at −70 mV.
claims.source: In summary, we found that when the CA2 PNs were kept at −70 mV, SuM input stimulation paired with SR or SLM input had a net depolarizing effect.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data from paired stimulation experiments.

claims.claim: For SR input stimulation, there was no significant difference between the observed paired SR+SuM amplitude and the calculated linear summated amplitude.
claims.source: For SR input stimulation, we found no significant difference between the observed paired SR+SuM amplitude and the calculated linear summated amplitude (SR alone + SuM alone) (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: For the SLM input stimulation, the observed paired amplitude was significantly smaller than the linear summation of the two inputs for the first stimulus.
claims.source: However, for the SLM input stimulation, the observed paired amplitude was significantly smaller than the linear summation of the two inputs (SLM alone + SuM alone) for the first stimulus (n = 10; T test, p=0.014) (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: There was a significant reduction of the summation ratio for both SR and SLM inputs when paired with SuM stimulation.
claims.source: We observed a significant reduction of the summation ratio as measured by the ratio of the n-th pulse to the first (Pn/P1) for both SR (n = 10; repeated-measures ANOVA, p=2.3×10−4) and SLM (n = 10; repeated-measures ANOVA, p=8.5×10−4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Concomitant SuM activity reduces the level of facilitation of several pulses in a train, preventing cellular excitation from other inputs.
claims.source: This observation that concomitant SuM activity is reducing the level of facilitation of several pulses in a train indicates that the short-term dynamics of the SuM-driven excitation and feedforward inhibition are playing a role to prevent cellular excitation from other inputs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on summation ratios.

claims.claim: Robust light-evoked excitatory transmission from SuM axons was observed in 35 out of 62 interneurons with soma located in SP.
claims.source: In contrast with previous reports of an exclusive innervation of PNs by SuM (Maglóczky et al., 1994), we observed robust light-evoked excitatory transmission from SuM axons in 35 out of 62 interneurons (INs) with soma located in SP.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from electrophysiological recordings.

claims.claim: 22 cells were classified as basket cells (BCs) because their axonal arborizations were restricted to SP.
claims.source: We classified 22 cells as basket cells (BCs) because their axonal arborizations were restricted to SP (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of recorded cells shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Light-evoked EPSCs and PSPs were readily observed in the vast majority of BCs.
claims.source: Light-evoked EPSCs and PSPs were readily observed in the vast majority of BCs (Figure 3A, C and D, Table 4) and reached large amplitudes in some instances.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figures and table.

claims.claim: 26 INs with soma in SP were classified as non-BCs because their axon did not target SP.
claims.source: An additional 26 INs with soma in SP were classified as non-BCs because their axon did not target SP (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis of recorded cells shown in the figure.

claims.claim: No or very minor light-evoked excitatory transmission was consistently observed onto non-BCs.
claims.source: We consistently observed no or very minor light-evoked excitatory transmission onto non-BCs (Figure 3B–C, Table 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figures and table.

claims.claim: SuM input preferentially forms excitatory synapses onto basket cells in area CA2.
claims.source: This data is consistent with the conclusion that SuM input preferentially forms excitatory synapses onto basket cells in area CA2.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing stronger connectivity and responses in BCs compared to other cell types.

claims.claim: BCs could fire action potentials upon SuM input photostimulation leading to a substantial feedforward inhibition of neighboring PNs.
claims.source: These BCs could fire action potentials upon SuM input photostimulation leading to a substantial feedforward inhibition of neighboring PNs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing AP firing in BCs and IPSCs in PNs.

claims.claim: At resting membrane potentials, the mixed excitatory/inhibitory SuM input resulted in a net depolarization of the membrane potential in CA2 PNs.
claims.source: We found that at resting membrane potentials, the mixed excitatory/inhibitory SuM input resulted in a net depolarization of the membrane potential in CA2 PNs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings at resting membrane potential.

claims.claim: When the SuM input was paired with either inputs in SR or SLM, there was a decrease in the summation ratios of trains of synaptic inputs consistent with a perisomatic shunting inhibition driven by SuM in area CA2.
claims.source: However, when the SuM input was paired with either inputs in SR or SLM, we observed a decrease in the summation ratios of trains of synaptic inputs consistent with a perisomatic shunting inhibition driven by SuM in area CA2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data from paired stimulation experiments.

claims.claim: With elevated cholinergic tone, recruitment of BCs by SuM controlled PNs excitability and shaped spontaneous burst firing.
claims.source: Furthermore, we found that with elevated cholinergic tone, recruitment of BCs by SuM controlled PNs excitability and shaped spontaneous burst firing.
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings in the presence of carbachol.

claims.claim: SuM activity can pace action potential firing in PNs through recruitment of feedforward inhibition.
claims.source: This finding demonstrates that SuM activity can pace action potential firing in PNs through recruitment of feedforward inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing reduced AP jitter with SuM stimulation.

claims.claim: The population of INs potently excited by SuM transmission display many features that classify them as PV+ BCs.
claims.source: The population of INs potently excited by SuM transmission display many features that motivate us to classify them as PV+ BCs.
claims.evidence: This is based on multiple lines of evidence including morphology, electrophysiology, and immunohistochemistry.

claims.claim: PV-immunoreactivity could unequivocally be detected in either the soma or dendrites of seven connected BCs.
claims.source: However, PV-immunoreactivity could unequivocally be detected in either the soma or dendrites of seven connected BCs (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: At least a fraction of the recorded BCs connected by the SuM is expressing PV.
claims.source: Therefore, this data demonstrates that at least a fraction of the recorded BCs connected by the SuM is expressing PV.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunohistochemical data.

claims.claim: The selective expression of GiDREADD in PV+ cells allows for selective silencing that reduces SuM-driven feedforward inhibition of area CA2 PNs.
claims.source: The selective expression of GiDREADD in PV+ cells allows for selective silencing that reduces SuM-driven feedforward inhibition of area CA2 PNs.
claims.evidence: This is supported by DREADD experiments showing reduced IPSCs with CNO application.

claims.claim: A substantial reduction of SuM-evoked IPSC amplitude was observed in area CA2 PNs upon application of 10 µM of the Gi-DREADD ligand CNO.
claims.source: We observed a substantial reduction of SuM-evoked IPSC amplitude recorded in area CA2 PNs upon application of 10 µM of the Gi-DREADD ligand CNO (Figure 5C; amplitudes were 847 ± 122 pA in control and 498 ± 87 pA in CNO hence a 42 ± 6.0% block, n = 13; paired-T test, p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacogenetic data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: PV+ cells are predominantly targeted by SuM inputs in area CA2.
claims.source: Altogether, these four methods strongly suggest that SuM inputs selectively recruit PV +interneurons to inhibit CA2 PNs. Although individually each method does not conclusively demonstrate that SuM input exclusively targets PV+ INs, the consistent reduction of SuM-driven feedforward inhibition of CA2 PNs observed with every approach allows us to conclude that PV + cells are predominantly targeted by SuM inputs in area CA2.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claims.claim: The feedforward inhibitory transmission recruited by SuM stimulation is highly sensitive to MOR activation.
claims.source: The feedforward inhibitory transmission recruited by SuM stimulation is highly sensitive to MOR activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data showing near complete block of IPSCs with DAMGO.

claims.claim: There was a near complete block of the light-evoked IPSC amplitude following 1 μM DAMGO application.
claims.source: We found that there was a near complete block of the light-evoked IPSC amplitude following 1 μM DAMGO application (Figure 5E 1; IPSC amplitudes were 343 ± 123 pA in control and 31 ± 12.4 pA in DAMGO hence a 88 ± 5.0% block, n = 6 PNs; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.031)
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Direct excitatory transmission remained unaffected by DAMGO application.
claims.source: while direct excitatory transmission remained unaffected (Figure 5E 2; EPSC amplitudes were −6.7 ± 1.1 pA in SR95531 and CGP55845A and −5.6 ± 0.9 pA after DAMGO, n = 17 PNs; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.19).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The SuM-recruited feedforward inhibition is sensitive to DOR activation.
claims.source: We also show that the SuM-recruited feedforward inhibition is sensitive to DOR activation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data showing reduction of IPSCs with DPDPE.

claims.claim: Application of 0.5 µM of the DOR agonist DPDPE led to a long-term reduction of light-evoked IPSCs recorded in area CA2 PNs.
claims.source: Application of 0.5 µM of the DOR agonist DPDPE led to a long-term reduction of light-evoked IPSCs recorded in area CA2 PNs, similar to the iLTD seen by CA3 input stimulation (Figure 5F 1; IPSC amplitudes were 168 ± 28 pA in control and 64 ± 22 pA in DPDPE hence a 61 ± 14% block by DPDPE, n = 7; paired-T test, p=0.015)
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Both the local CA3 and long-range SuM inputs converge onto an overlapping population of INs to inhibit area CA2 PNs.
claims.source: Further confirming the PV+ nature of INs responsible for the SuM feedforward inhibition, this result reveals that both the local CA3 and long-range SuM inputs converge onto an overlapping population of INs to inhibit area CA2 PNs, thus enabling cross-talk between these routes through synaptic plasticity of PV+ INs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DOR sensitivity data.

claims.claim: Recruitment of SuM inputs significantly delayed the onset of the first AP in CA2 PNs.
claims.source: We observed that recruitment of SuM inputs significantly delayed the onset of the first AP (Figure 6C; latency to the first AP were 221 ± 19.9 ms in control and 233 ± 19.1 ms with photostimulation, hence a 12.1 ± 4.3 ms increase upon photostimulation, n = 12; paired-T test, p=0.016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of SuM axons at 10 Hz led to a significant decrease of variability in the timing of AP firing by PNs.
claims.source: Indeed, photostimulation of SuM axons at 10 Hz led to a significant decrease of variability in the timing of AP firing by PNs (Figure 6D–E; standard deviations of the first AP timing were 36.9 ± 11 ms in control and 24.7 ± 7.4 ms with photostimulation, hence a 12.3 ± 5.3 ms decrease upon photostimulation, n = 12; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, p<0.001 for the first AP, p=0.008 for the second AP, p=0.004 for the third AP).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Both the delay of AP onset and the reduction of AP jitter stemmed from the feedforward inhibition recruited by SuM inputs.
claims.source: Both the delay of AP onset and the reduction of AP jitter stemmed from the feedforward inhibition recruited by SuM inputs as application of GABAA and GABAB receptor antagonists abolished these effects of SuM stimulation (Figure 6C–E; latency to the first AP were 232 ± 19.8 ms in SR95531 and CGP55845A and 235 ± 18.0 ms with photostimulation, n = 6; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.44; standard deviations of the first AP timing were 11.9 ± 2.0 ms in SR95531 and CGP55845A and 7.1 ± 1.5 ms with photostimulation, n = 6; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, p=0.22 for the first AP, p=0.16 for the second AP, p=0.09 for the third AP).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The purely glutamatergic SuM input, by recruiting feedforward inhibition, has an overall inhibitory effect on PN excitability.
claims.source: These results reveal that the purely glutamatergic SuM input, by recruiting feedforward inhibition, has an overall inhibitory effect on PN excitability and can influence the timing and jitter of area CA2 PN action potential firing.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing delayed and more precise AP firing with SuM stimulation.

claims.claim: The AP discharge of SuM neurons in vivo is phase-locked to the hippocampal theta rhythm.
claims.source: It has been reported that the AP discharge of SuM neurons in vivo is phase-locked to the hippocampal theta rhythm (Kocsis and Vertes, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claims.claim: CCh decreased the amplitude and increased the PPR of SuM-evoked EPSCs in CA2 PNs.
claims.source: With GABA receptors blocked to first assess the SuM excitatory transmission only, we observed that CCh decreased the amplitude and increased the PPR of SuM-evoked EPSCs in CA2 PNs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: CCh application decreased IPSC amplitude and increased PPR for SuM-evoked feedforward inhibitory transmission to CA2 PNs.
claims.source: We found similar results for SuM-evoked feedforward inhibitory transmission to CA2 PNs as IPSC amplitude was decreased and PPR increased with CCh application (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Both SuM-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs underwent short-term depression.
claims.source: We observed that both SuM-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs underwent short-term depression, as evidenced by a decrease in amplitude along the pulse train as well as amplitude ratios between subsequent pulses over the first pulse (Pn/P1) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The E/I ratio did not significantly change with repeated SuM input stimulation.
claims.source: It is worth noting that the Pn/P1 ratio was similar for EPSCs and IPSCs and that the E/I ratio did not significantly change with repeated SuM input stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F–G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The SuM influence over CA2 PN may remain overall inhibitory during prolonged SuM input activation.
claims.source: This indicates that the SuM influence over CA2 PN may remain overall inhibitory during prolonged SuM input activation.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the E/I ratio does not change significantly with repeated stimulation.

claims.claim: Application of 10 µM CCh decreased the amplitude of the initial response of SuM-evoked PSCs.
claims.source: Similarly influencing both EPSCs and IPSCs, application of 10 µM CCh affected these short-term dynamics of the SuM-CA2 PN transmission by decreasing the amplitude of the initial response (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1)
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: CCh application limited the subsequent short-term depression of SuM-evoked PSCs amplitude.
claims.source: Similarly influencing both EPSCs and IPSCs, application of 10 µM CCh affected these short-term dynamics of the SuM-CA2 PN transmission by decreasing the amplitude of the initial response (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1) but limiting the subsequent short-term depression of SuM-evoked PSCs amplitude (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: The E/I ratio of PSCs during the pulse train was lower in CCh as compared to control.
claims.source: Interestingly, the overall effect of repeated SuM input stimulation on post-synaptic responses in area CA2 PNs was even more biased toward inhibition after CCh application as the E/I ratio of PSCs during the pulse train was lower in CCh as compared to control (Figure 7—figure supplement 1G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1)
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: There was a significant decrease in the number of APs fired during a burst when SuM inputs were photostimulated as compared to interleaved control bursts.
claims.source: We observed a significant decrease in the number of APs fired during a burst when SuM inputs were photostimulated as compared to interleaved control bursts (Figure 7C–D; numbers of APs per burst were 15.2 ± 2.3 in control and 6.9 ± 1.3 with photostimulation, n = 7; paired-T test, p=0.031).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: In the photostimulation bursts, the initial increase of AP firing frequency was absent, and the subsequent AP firing frequency was reduced.
claims.source: In control bursts, the AP firing rate of CA2 PNs initially increases, and then progressively decreases. In the photostimulation bursts, the initial increase of AP firing frequency was absent, and the subsequent AP firing frequency was reduced (Figure 7E; two-way ANOVA on firing rate over time in light-on vs light-off conditions; light factor, p<0.001; time factor, p<0.001; light x time factor, p=0.052).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of SuM inputs resulted in a striking reduction in the amount of time the membrane potential remained depolarized.
claims.source: We observed that photostimulation of SuM inputs resulted in a striking reduction in the amount of time the membrane potential remained depolarized, and this is likely why the burst duration was significantly shorter in bursts with SuM photo-stimulation (Figure 7F–G; burst duration was 4.0 ± 1.1 s in control and 1.6 ± 0.5 s with photostimulation, n = 7; paired-T test, p=0.037).
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: AP bursts with SuM input activation were followed more rapidly by another burst of APs than the ones without SuM input activation.
claims.source: Indeed, AP bursts with SuM input activation were followed more rapidly by another burst of APs than the ones without SuM input activation (Figure 7B and H; time until next burst was 93 ± 14 s in control and 59 ± 17 s with photostimulation, n = 7; paired-T test, p=0.001)
claims.evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in the figure.

claims.claim: SuM input activation is able to modify the spontaneous bursting activity of CA2 PNs under conditions of high cholinergic tone.
claims.source: Thus, in our preparation, SuM input activation is able to modify the spontaneous bursting activity of CA2 PNs under conditions of high cholinergic tone.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing altered burst properties with SuM stimulation in the presence of carbachol.

claims.claim: The activation of SuM terminals in CA2 resulted in a significant and reproducible change in the multiunit spiking activity recorded in the pyramidal cell layer of CA1 on 34 of 55 tetrodes.
claims.source: Across 23 recording sessions in five mice, we found that the activation of SuM terminals in CA2 resulted in a significant and reproducible change in the multiunit spiking activity recorded in the pyramidal cell layer of CA1 on 34 of 55 tetrodes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by in vivo multi-unit recording data.

claims.claim: The firing rate change in CA1 showed a decrease starting shortly after laser onset and continuing for about 10 ms, followed immediately by a rebound-like increase to about 20% greater than baseline firing rate.

results.result: The authors characterize the anatomical projection pattern of SuM neurons to hippocampal area CA2 using viral tracing and immunohistochemistry. CA2-projecting SuM cells express calretinin and VGluT2, are located in the medial SuM, and their axons are restricted to area CA2 as defined by CA2-specific markers PCP4 and RGS14.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 are well-supported by anatomical data including viral tracing, immunohistochemistry, and imaging (Figures 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The findings are consistent with prior work (C39 cites Chen et al., 2020) and provide clear anatomical characterization of the SuM-CA2 projection.

results.result: SuM axon photostimulation elicits glutamatergic excitatory post-synaptic responses in 63% of pyramidal neurons in area CA2, with similar connectivity and amplitude across CA2/CA3 PNs and deep/superficial PNs. The responses are action potential-dependent and mediated by AMPA/NMDA receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C51 are supported by systematic electrophysiological recordings with appropriate controls (TTX, NBQX/D-APV) and statistical comparisons (Table 2, Figure 1). Sample sizes are adequate (n=166 of 263 cells) and the pharmacological validation confirms the glutamatergic nature of the transmission.

results.result: Blocking GABAergic inhibition with SR95531 and CGP55845A significantly increases SuM-evoked PSP amplitude in CA2 PNs, demonstrating that SuM-driven excitation is negatively controlled by feedforward inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are supported by pharmacological experiments with appropriate statistical analysis (Figure 2A-C, n=14, p-values reported for three PSPs). The conclusion of feedforward inhibition is well-justified by the increase in excitatory responses when inhibition is blocked.

results.result: SuM input paired with SR or SLM stimulation has a net depolarizing effect at -70 mV, but reduces summation ratios during trains of synaptic inputs, indicating that SuM-driven feedforward inhibition prevents cellular excitation from other inputs through perisomatic shunting.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by paired stimulation experiments with appropriate controls and statistical analysis (Figure 2D-H, n=10, repeated-measures ANOVA). The interpretation of shunting inhibition is consistent with the observed reduction in summation ratios and the known perisomatic location of basket cell synapses.

results.result: SuM inputs preferentially target basket cells (BCs) in area CA2, with 82% connectivity to BCs versus 39% to non-BCs. BCs receive significantly larger excitatory responses and can fire action potentials upon SuM stimulation, leading to feedforward inhibition of neighboring pyramidal neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 are well-supported by systematic electrophysiological recordings with morphological reconstruction (Figure 3, Table 4). The differential connectivity and response amplitudes are statistically significant (Kruskal-Wallis test, p<0.05), and the functional consequence of BC activation is demonstrated by AP firing in BCs but not other cell types.

results.result: The basket cells recruited by SuM inputs are predominantly parvalbumin-expressing (PV+) cells, as demonstrated by immunohistochemistry and DREADD-mediated silencing experiments showing 42% reduction in SuM-evoked IPSCs when PV+ cells are inhibited.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C75 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including immunohistochemistry (Figure 4C, n=7 cells), DREADD experiments (Figure 5C, n=13, p<0.001), and convergent pharmacological data. While individual methods have limitations (incomplete DREADD infection, partial PV staining), the consistent results across approaches support the conclusion.

results.result: SuM-recruited feedforward inhibition is highly sensitive to mu-opioid receptor (MOR) activation (88% block with DAMGO) and delta-opioid receptor (DOR) activation (61% block with DPDPE), with direct excitatory transmission remaining unaffected, indicating that both CA3 and SuM inputs converge onto overlapping PV+ interneuron populations.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C81 are supported by pharmacological experiments with appropriate controls (Figure 5E-F, n=6-17 cells, p<0.05). The selectivity for inhibitory versus excitatory transmission is clearly demonstrated, and the DOR sensitivity links SuM-recruited inhibition to the same PV+ population targeted by CA3 inputs.

results.result: SuM input stimulation at 10 Hz delays the onset of the first action potential by 12.1 ms and reduces AP timing variability (jitter) by 12.3 ms in CA2 PNs. These effects are mediated by feedforward inhibition and are abolished by GABA receptor antagonists.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are well-supported by electrophysiological recordings with appropriate controls (Figure 6, n=12 cells, paired t-tests and Wilcoxon tests with p<0.05). The mechanistic link to feedforward inhibition is confirmed by the abolition of effects with SR95531 and CGP55845A.

results.result: Under elevated cholinergic tone (carbachol), SuM-evoked EPSCs and IPSCs both undergo short-term depression with similar dynamics, maintaining a relatively constant E/I ratio. However, carbachol decreases initial response amplitudes while limiting subsequent depression, resulting in an overall more inhibitory influence during repeated stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C94 are supported by systematic analysis of short-term plasticity under carbachol (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, n=7-17 cells). The E/I ratio analysis is appropriate and the conclusion that SuM influence remains inhibitory during prolonged activation is justified by the data.

results.result: Under high cholinergic tone, SuM input stimulation at 10 Hz significantly reduces the number of APs per burst (from 15.2 to 6.9), eliminates the initial increase in firing frequency, shortens burst duration (from 4.0 to 1.6 s), and reduces inter-burst interval (from 93 to 59 s) in spontaneously bursting CA2 PNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 are well-supported by electrophysiological recordings in carbachol with interleaved control and stimulation trials (Figure 7, n=7 cells, paired t-tests with p<0.05). The experimental design with within-cell comparisons is appropriate and the statistical analysis is sound.

results.result: In vivo, SuM terminal stimulation in CA2 causes a reproducible decrease in CA1 multi-unit firing rate starting shortly after laser onset and lasting ~10 ms, followed by a rebound increase. Ex vivo recordings show that this is likely mediated by polysynaptic IPSCs in CA1 PNs occurring 10-20 ms after stimulation, with minimal direct excitatory input.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C105 are supported by converging in vivo (34 of 55 tetrodes, 5 mice, 23 sessions) and ex vivo (n=12 cells) data (Figure 8). The temporal correspondence between decreased firing in vivo and IPSCs ex vivo supports the mechanistic interpretation, though the polysynaptic nature introduces some uncertainty about intermediate circuit elements.

results.result: The main finding of the study: SuM axon stimulation elicits mixed excitatory and inhibitory responses in CA2 PNs, with PV+ basket cells mediating feedforward inhibition that enhances AP timing precision and controls CA2 output to CA1 through pulsed inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C8 and C106-C110 represent the core findings of the manuscript, which are supported by multiple converging lines of evidence including electrophysiology, pharmacology, immunohistochemistry, DREADD experiments, and in vivo recordings. The mechanistic model is well-supported by the data presented.

results.result: At resting membrane potential, SuM input causes net depolarization in CA2 PNs, but when paired with SR or SLM inputs, it produces perisomatic shunting inhibition. Under elevated cholinergic tone, SuM recruitment of BCs controls PN excitability and shapes spontaneous burst firing, demonstrating that SuM can pace AP firing through feedforward inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 integrate findings from multiple experimental conditions and are supported by the data in Figures 2, 6, and 7. The interpretation of shunting inhibition and pacing of AP firing is consistent with the known properties of perisomatic inhibition from PV+ basket cells.

results.result: Both intra-hippocampal CA3 inputs and long-range SuM inputs converge onto overlapping PV+ interneuron populations to control CA2 PN excitability and output.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 is supported by the DOR sensitivity data (C80-C81) showing that both inputs recruit the same population of PV+ INs that express DOR. This convergence is an important finding for understanding CA2 circuit integration.

results.result: Background claims establishing the importance of the hippocampus, area CA2, and SuM, as well as prior characterization of SuM projections and functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C9-C38, C86 are background claims supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These establish the context for the current study and are appropriately referenced.

results.result: Discussion of potential relevance to psychiatric disorders: PV+ INs in CA2 are lost in bipolar disorder, Alzheimer's disease, and schizophrenia. In a 22q11.2 deletion syndrome mouse model, there is loss of PV staining and deficits in inhibitory transmission and social memory. The authors speculate that disruption of the SuM-CA2 connection via PV+ IN dysfunction could contribute to cognitive impairments in schizophrenia.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C120 are primarily speculative (C118, C120) or cite prior work (C112-C116, C119). While the connection between the current findings and disease models is plausible, the manuscript does not provide direct experimental evidence linking SuM-CA2 circuit dysfunction to disease phenotypes. Claims C116-C117 provide some supporting data from the current study (DOR expression in SuM-targeted PV+ INs), but the overall disease relevance remains speculative.
